source_text: Exprimatur igitur vis argumentorum tuorum. Postquam dixit Paulus, quia multo magis abundasset gratia Salvatoris ad medendum quam praevaricatio primi hominis ad nocendum, sequitur: Et non sicut per unum peccantem ita est et donum; nam iudicium ex uno in condemnationem, gratia autem ex multis delictis in iustificationem [n144] . Quod tu delictum unum ad condemnationem sufficiens originale esse contendis in omnes videlicet homines pertransiens, gratiam autem ideo ex multis delictis in iustificationem dici, quia non solum illud unum solvit, quod originaliter trahitur, sed etiam cetera, quae in unoquoque homine motu propriae voluntatis adduntur [n145] . Ad quod confirmandum paulo post argumentaris, quia, si hoc unum delictum ad condemnationem sufficiens Apostolus dixisset imitatione susceptum, addere debuisset omnes homines ad condemnationem non per unum ire delictum, sed per multa sua quaeque voluntate commissa. In quibus locis quoniam elaqueandus est Apostoli sermo a cassibus Manichaeorum, ut sit attentus lector admoneo. Ais ergo secundum nostrum sensum, quo asseritur prima culpa formam praebuisse peccantibus, debuisse Apostolum, sicut gratiam ex multis delictis iustificationem dixit operari, ita ex multis peccatis dicere regnasse mortem. Porro hoc argumento contra te omnino luctaris; convinco enim secundum dogma tuum inconsequenter Apostolum pronuntiare: Gratia autem ex multis delictis in iustificationem, qui dixerat: Ex uno peccato iudicium in condemnationem. Ut enim egredientes de nostris finibus in vestra regione versemur: si libertas arbitrii primo est eversa peccato et in omni deinceps hominum genere manca adeo remansit, ut non sit ei possibile nisi tantummodo malum facere, non autem habeat in facultate electionem partis alterius, id est recedere a malo et facere bonum, sed iniquitatis necessitate depressa appetentiae criminum parere compellitur; si perrupta omni lege iustitiae facta sunt naturalia, quae fuerant voluntaria; si lex peccati habitat in membris, quae tyrannidem in imaginem et opus Dei nuptiarum verecundia et iucunditate sortita est; si frutex diaboli in visceribus pangitur ante animam et cum incrementis naturalibus adolescit, frondescit et pestifera fruge ingravescit; si haec, inquam, ut dicitis, una primi hominis culpa progenuit, consequentius dicitur ex uno delicto in condemnationem genus ire mortalium quam ex multis delictis gratiam liberare, ut magis proprie intellegatur dici posse haec gratia ex uno delicto liberare quos liberat. Nulla enim alia motu propriae voluntatis adduntur, si omne malum fracta arbitrii libertate, exclusa honestate desiderii infectrix seminum culpa primi genitoris operatur.
pass_a_gloss: Let therefore the force of your arguments be expressed. After Paul said that the Savior's grace had abounded much more toward healing than the transgression of the first human being toward harming, there follows: And not as through one sinning so also is the gift; for the judgment from one into condemnation, but grace from many offenses into justification. Which one offense sufficient for condemnation you contend is original, passing through namely into all human beings, but that grace is said therefore from many offenses into justification, because it not only looses that one which is drawn originally, but also the rest which in each human being are added by a motion of proper will. Toward confirming which a little later you argue that, if the Apostle had said this one offense sufficient for condemnation was taken up by imitation, he ought to have added that all human beings go unto condemnation not through one offense, but through many their own committed by will. In which places, since the Apostle's speech must be un-snared from the nets of the Manichaeans, I warn that the reader be attentive. You say therefore according to our sense, by which it is asserted that the first fault furnished a form to those sinning, that the Apostle ought, as he said that grace works justification from many offenses, so to say that death reigned from many sins. Further by this argument you wrestle altogether against yourself; for I convict that according to your dogma the Apostle pronounces inconsequently: But grace from many offenses into justification, who had said: From one sin judgment into condemnation. For that, going out from our borders, we may be turned in your region: if the freedom of decision was overturned by the first sin and thereafter remained so maimed in every kind of human beings that it is not possible for it except only to do evil, but does not have in faculty a choice of the other part, that is to withdraw from evil and do good, but, pressed down by a necessity of iniquity, is compelled to obey an appetite of crimes; if, every law of justice having been broken through, those things which had been voluntary were made natural; if the law of sin dwells in the members, which has obtained a tyranny over the image and work of God by the modesty and pleasantness of marriages; if the devil's shrub is planted in the inward parts before the soul and with natural increments grows up, puts out leaves, and grows heavy with pestiferous fruit; if these things, I say, as you say, one fault of the first human being brought forth, it is more consequently said that the race of mortals goes from one offense into condemnation than that grace frees from many offenses, so that it may be more properly understood that this grace can be said to free those whom it frees from one offense. For no others are added by a motion of proper will, if every evil, the freedom of decision having been broken, the honesty of desire having been excluded, is worked by the first begetter's fault that infects the seeds.

pass_b_english: Let us bring out the force of your arguments. After Paul said that the Savior’s grace abounded much more in healing than the first man’s transgression in harming, he continues: ‘And the gift is not as it was through one who sinned. For the judgment was from one to condemnation, but grace is from many offenses to justification’ (Romans 5:16). You contend that this one offense sufficient for condemnation is original sin, passing into all human beings. You say that grace is called ‘from many offenses to justification’ because it releases not only that one sin inherited at birth but also the other sins each person adds by the movement of his own will (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.46). A little later, to confirm this, you argue that, if the apostle had described this one offense sufficient for condemnation as acquired by imitation, he should have added that all people go to condemnation not through one offense, but through the many each has committed voluntarily. Since the apostle’s language must be disentangled here from the Manichaeans’ nets, I urge the reader to pay attention. You say that, according to our understanding—that the first fault supplied a model to sinners—the apostle ought to have said that death reigned through many sins, just as he said grace produces justification from many offenses. But with this argument you struggle entirely against yourself. I prove that, according to your doctrine, the apostle speaks inconsistently in saying, ‘But grace is from many offenses to justification,’ after saying, ‘The judgment was from one sin to condemnation.’ Let us leave our own territory and spend some time in yours. Suppose freedom of will was overthrown by the first sin, and thereafter remained so crippled throughout the human race that it can do nothing but evil; that it has no power to choose the other side—to turn from evil and do good (possible allusion to Psalm 34:14; compare Psalm 37:27 and 1 Peter 3:11)—but, oppressed by the necessity of wickedness, is compelled to obey a craving for crimes. Suppose that, with every law of justice broken, things once voluntary became natural; that the law of sin dwells in the limbs (Romans 7:23), having gained tyranny over God’s image and work through marriage’s modesty and pleasure; that the devil’s shrub is planted in the inner body before the soul arrives, and grows with natural growth, puts out leaves, and becomes heavy with deadly fruit. If, I say, the first man’s single fault produced all these things as you claim, it is more consistent to say that the mortal race goes into condemnation from one offense than that grace frees it from many offenses. One should more properly understand this grace as freeing those it frees from one offense. For no other sins are added by the movement of a personal will if all evil is worked by the first parent’s fault that infects the seed, with freedom of will broken and honorable desire excluded.
